title: Convert printf calls individually with flush barriers instead of all-or-nothing
description:
Why: printf_format::fixup currently bails on the ENTIRE program if even one printf call anywhere uses an unsupported conversion (has_unsupported_printf in src/fixups/rewrite/printf_format.rs:9-11, checked program-wide against facts.printf_calls). This means one unsupported format specifier anywhere blocks every other convertible printf in the program from becoming println!/print!, even when they have nothing to do with each other.

What to do:
- Change the gating to per-call: only skip conversion for calls that individually fail arg_supports_conversion/parse_printf_format, not the whole program.
- Mixing libc::printf and println!/print! in the same binary is only safe if byte order to fd 1 is preserved: Rust's Stdout is unconditionally line-buffered (flushes per \n regardless of tty-ness), while C's stdio defaults to fully buffered when stdout isn't a tty (the differential harness's case), so an unconverted libc::printf's bytes can otherwise land out of program order relative to surrounding println!/print! output.
- Fix: wrap every call that remains a raw libc::printf with a flush barrier -- std::io::stdout().flush() immediately before it, libc::fflush(stdout) immediately after it -- so relative ordering across the two buffering disciplines is pinned to program order.
- Keep prune_printf_extern's condition working with partial conversion (only prune the libc printf extern decl if zero raw calls remain after per-call conversion).
acceptance_criteria: Programs with a mix of convertible and unconvertible printf calls get the convertible ones turned into println!/print!, and the unconvertible ones stay as libc::printf wrapped in the flush barriers. A differential fixture exercises this: some printf calls with fully-supported formats alongside at least one with an unsupported conversion, interleaved with an already-existing println!/print!-only call, verifying stdout ordering matches the C reference exactly. Existing printf_format tests and the full differential suite still pass.

title: Recover lazy-init singletons as OnceLock/LazyLock
description:
Why: the 'static local guarded by an initialized flag' idiom (if (!initialized) { init(); initialized = true; }) is a common C lazy-singleton pattern. Baseline lowering keeps it as static mut plus unsafe flag checks; Rust has a direct safe equivalent.

What to do:
- New fact: a static local is guarded by a boolean 'initialized' flag with no other writer, and the guarded body is the only place that mutates the static.
- Rewrite: replace with std::sync::OnceLock::get_or_init (or LazyLock where the init has no runtime args).
- Narrow pattern but removes real unsafe/static mut where it appears; low interaction risk with other passes.
acceptance_criteria: Fact collector proves the guard-flag/single-writer shape. Rewrite emits OnceLock/LazyLock usage. Differential tests pass; fixture covers both the singleton path and a case where the guard can't be proven safe (must stay on baseline path).
notes: Implemented as a fact+rewrite pass e2e. Touches: src/fixups/facts/lazy_singleton.rs (new), src/fixups/rewrite/lazy_singleton.rs (new), src/fixups/facts/mod.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/mod.rs, src/fixups/mod.rs, tests/differential.rs, tests/fixtures/lazy_singleton.c, tests/fixtures/lazy_singleton_unsafe_alias.c. Scope note: only integer-typed (non-bool) scalar payloads are recognized, to sidestep two pre-existing unrelated baseline bugs (address-of file-scope struct statics, and bool-typed static lowering) discovered during development.
close_reason: Implemented fact+rewrite pass pair; merged to main at 2ae2e32. All acceptance criteria met: fact collector proves guard-flag/single-writer shape program-wide, rewrite emits OnceLock::get_or_init, differential tests pass with both a qualifying fixture and a non-qualifying (aliased-read) fixture staying on baseline. Full nextest suite (577 tests) green.

title: Recover 3-statement temp-swaps as slice.swap()
description:
Why: the classic 'tmp = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = tmp;' swap idiom appears constantly in sort/search C code. Once a[j] is a slice (post slice_index), this is a direct, zero-risk mapping to the native slice.swap(i, j) method.

What to do:
- New fact: a 3-statement sequence over an already-lifted slice matching the temp-swap shape (single-use temp, same slice on both sides, indices used exactly once each in the expected positions).
- Rewrite: replace the 3 statements with a single slice.swap(i, j) call.
- Self-contained, single-function, low blast radius — good first-pass candidate alongside the out-param ticket. Slots naturally after slice_index/slice_loop in the pass sequence.
acceptance_criteria: Fact/rewrite recognizes the swap shape only when the slice and indices are already proven (post slice_index). Differential tests pass; fixture includes qsort/bsearch-adjacent swap patterns and a near-miss case that must not be rewritten (e.g. tmp reused elsewhere).

title: Recover bitflag idioms as named flag constants
description:
Why: C code commonly ORs/ANDs a closed set of power-of-two #define/enum constants into an int (permission bits, option flags, etc). Baseline lowering keeps this as bare integer bitwise ops with no semantic naming, unlike printf or string idioms which already get a dedicated recovery rung.

What to do:
- New fact: an integer local/field is only ever touched via |=, &=, or & against a small closed set of power-of-two constants (from #define or enum).
- Rewrite: at minimum, emit typed const masks with the original names instead of bare int literals; consider a bitflags!-style newtype with named methods (contains/insert/remove) if it composes cleanly with existing type recovery.
- Lower payoff than the out-param/Result/tagged-union tickets but mechanical and low-risk — good candidate for after those land.
acceptance_criteria: Fact collector identifies closed power-of-two constant sets used bitwise on a single binding. Rewrite emits named constants (or bitflags-style wrapper) in place of bare literals. Differential tests pass; no change in emitted bit values.

title: Document nullable_pointer (33) producer dependency
description: pass-considerations.md item #4 speculated nullable_pointer (step 33) was isolated from the pointer-provenance cluster with no stated reason for its position. Investigation showed it has a real, previously undocumented producer dependency: it consumes the .map_or(null_mut(), ...) shape emitted only by string_libc::fixup and memchr_prelude::fixup_calls (32), and has no relationship to the constant-index pointer-provenance passes despite the similar name.
close_reason: Doc-only fix: documented nullable_pointer's real producer dependency (string_libc::fixup + memchr_prelude::fixup_calls) in docs/passes.md step 33, confirmed no relationship to pointer-provenance cluster, removed item #4 from pass-considerations.md. No code change, no worktree needed.

title: Collapse repeated prune_unused_externs calls into one final pass
description: pass-considerations.md #5: string_copy, string_libc (x2), sort_search, and heap_ownership each carry their own prune_unused_externs call in fixups::apply, run right after their respective fixup. All four share the same shape (retain extern decls whose name isn't in a fixed allow-list unless still called per FixupFacts.callsites). None of the fixup() passes in between inspect ExternBlock presence to make rewrite decisions -- only direct_calls facts. So the pruning is cosmetic dead-code cleanup, not a correctness dependency, and can be collapsed into a single generalized prune pass run once at the end of the pipeline (near unused_items), rather than 5 separate call sites across fixups::mod.rs.
design: Combine the four narrow allow-lists (strcpy family, strlen/strcmp family, qsort/bsearch, malloc/calloc/realloc/free) into one shared prune_unused_externs(program, facts) run once after all rewrite passes (right before or alongside unused_items::fixup). Remove the 5 existing call sites in src/fixups/mod.rs. Verify no fixup() between steps 24-42 inspects Item::ExternBlock presence to decide behavior (only calls.rs/casts.rs facts read signatures for type info, unaffected by pruning timing).
acceptance_criteria: cargo nextest r --release passes with identical results; docs/passes.md and pass-considerations.md updated to reflect the single end-of-pipeline prune pass.
notes: touches: src/fixups/mod.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/string_copy.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/string_libc.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/sort_search.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/heap_ownership.rs, docs/passes.md, pass-considerations.md
close_reason: Collapsed the 5 per-rewrite prune_unused_externs call sites (string_copy, string_libc x2, sort_search, heap_ownership) into one rewrite::prune_unused_externs pass run near the end of the pipeline, after confirming no intervening pass reads ExternBlock presence to decide behavior. 572/572 tests pass; docs/passes.md and pass-considerations.md updated.

title: Consolidate fact-struct site fields into a shared Site struct
description: Sixteen fact structs in src/fixups/facts/ (EffectFact, ControlFlowFact, CastFact, PlaceFact, ValueFact, CallsiteFact, StringBufferFact, AsciiNumericStringFact, StringPointerViewFact, StringLibcUseFact, StringLiftPlanFact, StringCopyRewriteFact, PrintfCallFact, ArrayElementPointerOriginFact, SlicePointerViewFact, SlicePointerIndexFact) each duplicated the same (function: FunctionId, path: AstPath) pair used to key lookups. Introduced a shared Site struct (mirroring the existing LoopSite precedent) and threaded it through all 16 structs, their collectors, and their consumers.
design: Site { function: FunctionId, path: AstPath } embedded as a named field (site: Site) rather than flattened, matching the LoopSite pattern already used for loop facts.
acceptance_criteria: cargo build and cargo nextest r --release both pass with no regressions (572/572); cargo fmt applied.

title: Preserve sizeof alignof and offsetof as Rust std::mem calls
description:
Why: Slate currently lowers compile-time layout queries like sizeof(struct Aligned), _Alignof(struct Aligned), and offsetof(struct Aligned, field) to numeric constants. That preserves output but loses useful type-level layout intent in the generated Rust.

What to do: Recover these layout queries as std::mem::size_of::<T>(), std::mem::align_of::<T>(), and std::mem::offset_of!(T, field) where Slate can prove the constant came from the corresponding source-level query. The aligned_struct fixture should render the std::mem forms instead of raw u64 constants.

Acceptance: Add failing output-shape coverage for aligned_struct, implement the lowering/fixup path without changing behavior, and verify with cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, cargo fmt, and cargo nextest r --release.
notes: touches: src/lower.rs, src/c_ast.rs or src/fixups/, tests/differential.rs, tests/fixtures/aligned_struct.c
close_reason: Implemented layout query preservation with std::mem lowering and validated on merged main.

title: Hoist unobserved struct field assignments into initializers
description:
Why: Slate currently lowers a pattern like struct Aligned s; followed by s.a = 5; and s.b = 0x1234; into a zero/default struct initializer followed by field assignments. When no operation observes the partially initialized value between those assignments, the assignments can be folded into the initializer, which then allows later remove-mut cleanup to make the binding immutable.

What to do: Add a Rust AST fixup that recognizes a local mutable struct binding initialized with a struct literal/default-field literal, followed immediately by field assignments to fields on the same local, with no intervening reads or side effects. Fold those field values into the initializer and leave unsupported shapes unchanged. The pass must operate on AST nodes, not rendered text, and should use shared fixup traversal helpers where applicable.

Acceptance: Add unit coverage for the fold and conservative non-fold cases, add or update fixture output-shape coverage for an aligned struct example, keep differential behavior unchanged, and verify with cargo fmt plus the relevant test suite.
notes: touches: src/fixups/, src/fixups/mod.rs, tests/fixtures/, tests/differential.rs
close_reason: Implemented a Rust AST fixup that folds consecutive unobserved struct field assignments into struct literals, enabling remove-mut on the aligned_struct fixture. Verified with cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, cargo fmt, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Lower __attribute__((alias("target"))) via forwarding wrapper
description:
Why: __attribute__((alias("target"))) makes one symbol name an alias for another already-defined symbol -- used for versioned symbols, ABI compatibility shims, and multiple names for one implementation. CIR encodes this directly (aliasee = @target attr plus an empty region on the aliased cir.func/cir.global), so detection is trivial, but Rust has no native symbol-aliasing construct comparable to LLVM's @llvm.alias.

What to do:
- Detect alias from CIR: an item with an aliasee attr and an empty region is an alias for the named target; the target is looked up among already-lowered items in the same translation unit.
- Lower as a thin forwarding item rather than true pointer-identical aliasing: for functions, emit #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn alias_name(...) matching signature that calls target(...) and returns its result; for globals/statics, this is trickier since Rust has no forwarding-static construct -- likely needs a #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub static ALIAS: T = ... duplicate-value approach, OR diagnose global aliasing as unsupported if no faithful non-pointer-identical representation exists (decide during implementation; document the chosen tradeoff).
- This does not achieve true pointer identity (&alias_name != &target address-wise for globals in the wrapper-function case for functions this is fine since call forwarding preserves observable behavior) -- Slate's correctness bar is observable behavior (stdout/exit code) per project charter, not pointer/address identity, so function aliasing via forwarding is acceptable; flag the global-aliasing case explicitly as a design risk to resolve before implementation.
- If the aliasee target is external (e.g. aliasing a libc symbol not defined in this translation unit), diagnose as unsupported and fall back conservatively rather than emitting a call to an undefined Rust item.
design: CIR source of truth: aliasee = @target string attr + empty region on cir.func/cir.global, confirmed via direct CIR dump inspection -- no AST JSON needed for detection. The open design question is global/static aliasing representation; function aliasing via a forwarding wrapper is well-defined and matches the project's existing diagnose-and-fallback pattern (jep.1/jep.3 precedent) for anything not cleanly representable.
acceptance_criteria: Fixture: a C function alias (__attribute__((alias("real_impl")))) lowers to a forwarding wrapper function; differential test confirms identical stdout/exit code calling through the alias name versus the real name. Global/static aliasing either has a working fixture or an explicit diagnostic-and-fallback fixture, whichever design is chosen during implementation -- document the decision in docs/idiomatization.md or an equivalent doc. cargo fmt/cargo nextest r --release green.
close_reason: Implemented function alias lowering as C ABI forwarding wrappers, diagnosed unsupported global aliases, documented the tradeoff, and verified with cargo fmt plus cargo nextest r --release.

title: Lower __attribute__((used)) and __attribute__((retain)) via #[used]/#[used(compiler)]/#[used(linker)]
description:
Why: __attribute__((used)) and __attribute__((retain)) tell the compiler/linker to keep a symbol alive even though nothing in the translation unit references it -- common for ISR tables, linker-script-collected registration arrays, and weak-symbol placeholders. Slate's unused_items.rs dead-code fixup pass currently has no notion of 'must retain,' so it can and will prune Rust items that the C source explicitly demanded be kept alive, silently changing behavior (e.g. a dropped ISR table entry).

Investigation performed: read CIRGenModule.cpp (setCommonAttributes/setNonAliasAttributes/addUsedGlobal/addCompilerUsedGlobal) directly. used routes through a synthesized llvm.compiler.used CIR global; retain routes through a SEPARATE synthesized llvm.used CIR global. Both are populated correctly and independently by CIR today -- confirmed by testing __attribute__((retain)) int external_retained together with __attribute__((used, retain)) static int used_and_retained: both correctly appear in llvm.used, and used_and_retained also appears in llvm.compiler.used, exactly matching LLVM's dual-list semantics. There is no CIR gap and no llvm.used-swap-in workaround is needed.

Important nuance confirmed against Clang's own AttrDocs.td (RetainDocs): retain ALONE on a symbol the compiler would otherwise eliminate (e.g. an unreferenced static) has NO EFFECT by design -- retain only prevents linker section garbage collection (SHF_GNU_RETAIN) on symbols already being emitted for another reason (typically paired with used, or already externally linked). This is standard, intentional Clang/GCC behavior, not a bug to work around. Slate's lowering and fixtures must reflect this: a retain-only-on-a-dead-static fixture is expected to correctly disappear, matching C's own behavior.

What to do:
- Detect used vs retain per-symbol from CIR by checking membership in the synthesized llvm.compiler.used / llvm.used globals (or, if simpler, from the AttrDocs-documented source attrs directly if CIR preserves UsedAttr/RetainAttr as boolean attrs on the item itself -- verify which is more direct during implementation).
- Add Attr::Used(UsedKind) to src/rust_ast.rs where UsedKind is Compiler (used) or Linker (retain), or a plain Attr::Used for the simple case if #[used] (stable, no compiler/linker distinction) is sufficient -- decide during implementation whether the compiler/linker distinction is worth the nightly feature cost.
- If the compiler/linker distinction is implemented: gate with #![feature(used_with_arg)] at the crate root (nightly is acceptable per project decision) and render #[used(compiler)] / #[used(linker)] respectively (edition 2024 unsafe() wrapping needs verification per attribute -- test both empirically before finalizing codegen).
- Update src/fixups/unused_items.rs so items carrying Attr::Used (any kind) are never pruned by the dead-code elimination pass, regardless of whether anything in the lowered Rust references them.
design: CIR carries used and retain as two independent synthesized top-level globals (llvm.compiler.used, llvm.used respectively), both appending arrays of cir.global_view<@name> entries with linkage=6 (Appending) and section="llvm.metadata". This is CIR-native; no AST JSON fallback required for the documented/idiomatic case.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures: (1) used-only static that would otherwise be dead-code-eliminated by unused_items.rs survives and is annotated #[used]/#[used(compiler)]; verified present in the compiled binary's symbol table even though unreferenced. (2) used+retain together survive and carry both markers. (3) retain-only on an otherwise-dead static is a no-op matching C's own documented behavior (no crash, no false 'unsupported' diagnostic -- this must NOT regress into an incorrect always-keep-alive rule). cargo fmt/cargo nextest r --release green.
notes: This ticket also owns the unused_items.rs cross-cutting fix -- do not let alias/weak/section tickets touch that pass.
close_reason: Implemented lowering for used/retain globals and added cross-TU coverage

title: Lower __attribute__((weak)) via #[linkage = "weak"]
description:
Why: __attribute__((weak)) marks a symbol as weakly linked -- the linker picks a strong definition over a weak one if both exist, or silently drops the weak one if unreferenced. This is used for optional overridable hooks and default/fallback implementations, common in C libraries. Rust's #[linkage = "weak"] is nightly-gated but the project is on a nightly toolchain, so it is available -- this reverses an earlier draft plan to diagnose-and-drop weak, made obsolete by the nightly-features-are-fine decision.

What to do:
- Detect weak linkage from CIR: linkage attr == 4 (WeakAnyLinkage), confirmed empirically against LLVM's GlobalValue::LinkageTypes encoding.
- Add Attr::Linkage(String) (or a dedicated Attr::Weak) to src/rust_ast.rs; render as #[linkage = "weak"] in src/codegen.rs.
- Gate with #![feature(linkage)] at the crate root when any weak item is present (only emit the crate-level feature attribute when needed, to avoid polluting every generated crate).
- weak items are necessarily also externally linked (C's weak implies external linkage in the absence of static weak, which is rare/questionable) -- compose with the no_mangle ticket's output rather than duplicating the external-linkage visibility logic.
- Confirm interaction with used/retain and section attributes composes correctly (a symbol can be weak AND used AND sectioned simultaneously) -- attribute rendering in codegen.rs must support stacking multiple Attr variants on one item, which the existing Attr enum design already allows.
design: CIR linkage attr numeric encoding confirmed: WeakAnyLinkage=4. Verified #[linkage = "weak"] combined with #[unsafe(no_mangle)] compiles cleanly on local nightly (rustc 1.99.0-nightly) under --edition 2024.
acceptance_criteria: Fixture: a C function and a C global declared __attribute__((weak)) lower to #[linkage = "weak"] #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub ...; differential test compiles and links successfully. A second fixture with both a weak and a strong definition of the same symbol (two translation units or a differential-test-appropriate equivalent) confirms the strong definition wins at link time, matching C linker semantics. cargo fmt/cargo nextest r --release green.
close_reason: Implemented weak linkage lowering with #[linkage = "weak"], project-level feature gating, and cross-TU/linker coverage. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Lower __attribute__((section("..."))) via #[unsafe(link_section = "...")]
description:
Why: __attribute__((section(...))) places a function or global into a specific ELF section, a common pattern for embedded linker scripts, interrupt vector tables, and custom registration tables (e.g. __attribute__((section(".init_array"))) constructor tables). Slate currently drops this attribute entirely, silently producing Rust that links into the default section -- for embedded/systems C this can change correctness (wrong memory region) not just layout.

What to do:
- Read the section attr directly off cir.func / cir.global (confirmed present verbatim as a string attr, e.g. section = ".mysection"): no AST JSON needed.
- Add Attr::LinkSection(String) to src/rust_ast.rs and render as #[unsafe(link_section = "...")] in src/codegen.rs (edition 2024 requires the unsafe() wrapper, same as no_mangle).
- Applies to both function and static/global items.
- No diagnostic-fallback case is needed for the common case: section is a plain string attr CIR always carries verbatim when present.
design: Source of truth: CIR section attr, string-valued, present directly on cir.func/cir.global. This is the simplest of the jep.4 sub-attributes -- a 1:1 syntactic mapping with no semantic gap versus C.
acceptance_criteria: Fixture: a function and a global each with __attribute__((section(".custom_section"))) lower to #[unsafe(link_section = "...")]; compiled Rust binary's section table (readelf -S / objdump) shows the symbol placed in the expected section, matching the C reference build. cargo fmt/cargo nextest r --release green.
close_reason: Implemented Attr::LinkSection rendered as #[unsafe(link_section = ...)] and lowered CIR section attrs for functions/globals. Added cross-TU fixture coverage asserting generated Rust and readelf section tables for C/Rust binaries. Verified with cargo test --test cross_tu cross_tu_globals -- --nocapture, cargo test --test cross_tu, cargo fmt, git diff --check, and cargo nextest r --release on work/slate-jep.9 before merge.

title: Use malloc, alloc_size, alloc_align, and assume_aligned attributes as allocation facts
description:
Why: allocation-related attributes describe ownership, returned pointer provenance, size, and alignment. They can improve heap ownership, slice recovery, and alignment-sensitive lowering, but should not change baseline behavior unless the contract is explicit.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for malloc-like functions with alloc_size, alloc_align, and assume_aligned attributes.
- Extract facts from AST/CIR and expose them to heap/pointer analysis.
- Use the facts in later fixups only when calls and lifetimes match the allocation contract.

Acceptance: allocation fact extraction has focused tests; at least one fixture demonstrates a consuming improvement or documented future consumer; ambiguous attributes remain facts only.

title: Lower linkage, visibility, weak, alias, used, retain, and section attributes
description:
Why: symbol attributes affect linkage and whether generated libraries expose, retain, or alias C symbols. These matter for real C libraries and embedded-style registration tables.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for visibility, weak, alias, used/retain, and section on functions/globals.
- Determine which facts are available from Clang AST JSON versus CIR attrs.
- Map to Rust/linker attributes where stable and target-appropriate: #[no_mangle], #[export_name], #[link_section], visibility, and retention patterns.
- Diagnose unsupported alias/weak combinations rather than emitting misleading Rust.

Acceptance: compile/link-shape tests verify emitted symbols/sections where feasible; unsupported cases produce clear diagnostics; docs record target limitations.
notes: Split into six focused sub-tickets under slate-jep, each independently scoped and with its own fixtures/acceptance: slate-jep.8 (no_mangle/external linkage, foundational), slate-jep.9 (section), slate-jep.10 (used/retain), slate-jep.11 (weak), slate-jep.12 (alias), slate-jep.13 (visibility, best-effort). jep.9 through jep.13 all depend on jep.8 since they attach to an already-correctly-exported symbol.

title: Use nonnull and returns_nonnull attributes in pointer lowering facts
description:
Why: nonnull attributes are source-level contracts that can justify Option/reference recovery and remove null checks, but violating them is UB in C. Slate should preserve them as baseline facts first, then let fixups consume them only under explicit proof rules.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for parameter nonnull indexes, returns_nonnull, and null-passing UB avoidance cases.
- Extract attribute facts and attach them to function signatures/call facts.
- Keep baseline pointer lowering correct while exposing the facts to nullable-pointer and pointer-to-reference fixups.
- Document the UB-preserving assumption boundary.

Acceptance: fact tests cover accepted and rejected nonnull positions; generated output remains behaviorally equivalent; consuming fixups only use facts where sound.

title: Recover safe slice idioms for builtin memory operations on proven local buffers
description:
Why: Slate has baseline CIR memory-op handling for builtin memcpy/memmove/memset/memchr shapes, and memchr has one idiom ticket. Fixed local-buffer copies and fills can often become safe slice operations, reducing unsafe pointer calls without changing correctness.

What to do:
- Start from fixtures that already lower through cir.libc.memcpy/memmove/memset.
- Add facts proving destination/source are local arrays or lifted slices, byte counts fit, and overlap rules match memcpy versus memmove.
- Rewrite only proven cases to copy_from_slice, copy_within/copy_from_slice, or fill-style operations as appropriate.
- Leave ambiguous pointer/provenance cases on the baseline std::ptr path.

Assumption: safe slice rewrites require exact provenance, length, and overlap proof; otherwise baseline unsafe pointer operations are the correct fallback.
acceptance_criteria: Output-shape tests cover accepted memcpy, memmove, and memset rewrites plus rejected overlapping/unknown-pointer near misses; differential tests stay green.

title: Add builtin dynamic object-size query support
description:
Why: Slate handles __builtin_object_size through cir.objsize, but modern fortified C often uses __builtin_dynamic_object_size. It may produce a different CIR shape or stay as a builtin call, and Slate should handle the common folded cases.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for __builtin_dynamic_object_size on local arrays, pointer offsets, globals, and unknown pointers.
- Inspect CIR and Clang AST facts for each mode.
- Reuse the existing object-size machinery where semantics match; otherwise add a conservative lowering that matches Clang's runtime/fallback result for the supported subset.

Assumption: only deterministic, target-stable object-size cases should be idiomatized; unknown dynamic sizes keep the Clang-compatible sentinel behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures cover known local/global sizes and unknown pointers; output matches C for all four object-size modes where supported; docs note any unsupported dynamic cases; cargo nextest r --release passes.

title: Support stack allocation builtins with a conservative Rust representation
description:
Why: __builtin_alloca and aligned variants appear in C projects and do not map cleanly to safe Rust stack allocation. Slate needs an explicit policy instead of falling through to generic unsupported calls.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for __builtin_alloca and any CIR stack allocation op emitted by the toolchain.
- Choose a conservative representation, likely a scoped Vec<u8> / MaybeUninit buffer or an intentional unsupported diagnostic when lifetime/provenance cannot be preserved.
- Treat aligned alloca separately if alignment is observable.

Assumption: heap-backed emulation is acceptable only when pointer lifetime and alignment remain behaviorally equivalent for Slate's supported subset.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures either translate through a documented conservative representation or fail with an intentional diagnostic; no silent incorrect stack-lifetime emulation; tests cover lifetime escape rejection if implemented.

title: Add missing scalar math builtin coverage for fma/hypot/fdim/cbrt and scaling/logb families
description:
Why: Slate handles many math builtins and stdlib probes, but common scalar math builtins such as __builtin_fma, __builtin_hypot, __builtin_fdim, __builtin_cbrt, __builtin_ldexp/scalbn, and logb/ilogb-style families need explicit builtin fixtures and lowering decisions. Some may lower as CIR ops, others as builtin calls.

What to do:
- Add focused __builtin_* fixtures separate from plain libc math probes.
- Inspect CIR for each spelling and implement Rust method/function equivalents only where C/Rust semantics are close enough for the test contract.
- Keep errno/fenv-sensitive or long-double cases on conservative helper/libc paths unless Slate already models the needed ABI.

Assumption: idiomatic Rust math is valid only for deterministic scalar cases where errno and floating-point environment side effects are irrelevant to the program.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures cover at least fma, hypot, fdim, cbrt, ldexp/scalbn, and logb/ilogb builtin spellings accepted by Clang; supported cases lower to Rust idioms or documented helpers; rejected long-double/fenv-sensitive cases are explicit; differential tests pass.

title: Support __builtin_assume_aligned and recover aligned pointer facts
description:
Why: __builtin_assume_aligned is common in vectorized C and can justify cleaner Rust around pointer alignment, but blindly trusting it is unsafe. Slate needs baseline handling plus optional facts that downstream fixups can use.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for __builtin_assume_aligned(p, n) and, if CIR/Clang supports it, the offset form.
- Lower the value conservatively as the original pointer while recording the asserted alignment fact where source/CIR facts expose it.
- Let later pointer/slice fixups consume the alignment fact only when provenance, type, and lifetime are already proven.

Assumption: the aligned result is valid only if the C program's alignment promise is true.
acceptance_criteria: A fixture translates without todo output; alignment assertions are represented as facts or documented source facts; ambiguous uses remain raw pointers; differential tests and focused fact tests pass.

title: Support branch-hint builtins beyond __builtin_expect
description:
Why: Slate already lowers cir.expect by returning the value, which is the right conservative Rust behavior for branch prediction hints. Clang also exposes related hint builtins such as __builtin_expect_with_probability and __builtin_unpredictable in real C code.

What to do:
- Add fixtures for the related branch-hint builtins that the CIR toolchain accepts.
- Inspect whether they lower to cir.expect, another CIR op, or ordinary calls.
- Lower them to the hinted expression value while preserving side effects and types.
- Do not invent runtime checks; these are optimization hints.

Assumption: branch probability metadata may be erased because Rust has no stable equivalent with required semantics.
acceptance_criteria: Supported branch-hint builtins translate to the original value expression, side-effecting operands still execute exactly once, unsupported forms are tracked with diagnostics, and differential tests pass.

title: Idiomatize remaining useful Clang builtins
description:
Why: Slate already handles many Clang builtin CIR shapes, but several common builtin families either drop semantic assumptions too aggressively or still have no dedicated Rust idiom path. These should be tracked under the fixup epic because the baseline must remain correct and conservative, while optional fixups can recover Rust forms when explicit proof assumptions are met.

What to do:
- Add focused C fixtures for each builtin family before implementation.
- Preserve the baseline/fixup split: correctness in lowering, readability and safe idioms in fixups.
- Only emit unsafe Rust idioms such as core::hint::assert_unchecked when the generated code intentionally preserves the C builtin UB contract.
- Keep unsupported or ambiguous builtin shapes on conservative raw-pointer/libc/no-op paths with diagnostics where appropriate.
acceptance_criteria: A child bead exists for each selected builtin family, each child states the required assumptions and verification plan, and implemented children include differential fixtures plus output-shape assertions where stable.

title: Inline final atomic print aliases
description: Why: generated atomics.rs still leaves tail aliases like let _v30 = loaded; println!(..., _v30) even though the source bindings are immutable and safe to read directly. What to do: teach the late temp cleanup to remove simple immutable var-to-var aliases after atomic fixups without changing behavior. Verify: atomics.rs print path no longer contains these redundant aliases; full suite green.
acceptance_criteria: Redundant tail aliases in tests/fixtures.generated/atomics.rs disappear; real uses of mutable/effectful values are preserved; cargo nextest r --release passes.
close_reason: Added a late var-alias cleanup pass that removes single-use _v aliases after atomics and verified atomics.rs no longer has the tail aliases.

title: Add atomics to the differential fuzzer generator and c.bnf
description:
Why: per project convention the generator emits everything Slate can translate; atomics are translated but tests/support/cgen.rs and c.bnf don't cover them, so the fuzzer never stresses this surface (mixed op sequences, width/signedness interaction, ordering variants).

What to do: extend tests/support/cgen.rs to generate well-defined single-threaded atomic programs — declare _Atomic integer locals, emit random sequences of store/load/fetch_add/sub/and/or/xor/exchange/compare_exchange_strong with printed results, constrain operands to avoid signed overflow UB (same discipline the generator already uses for plain arithmetic). Add the corresponding productions to c.bnf. Gate generation on the ops the lowerer supports; skip float/pointer atomics until their fallback shape is fuzz-safe.

Verify: SLATE_FUZZ_SEED-replayable runs of 'cargo nextest r --release --test bnf_fuzz generator_differential' pass with atomics enabled.

Depends on the lowerer/fixup children landing first so the fuzzer isn't chasing known density bugs.
acceptance_criteria:
- cgen.rs generates atomic op sequences with no UB.
- c.bnf documents the atomic productions.
- Fuzz differential runs pass repeatedly (multiple seeds).
close_reason: Added single-threaded integer atomic generation to tests/support/cgen.rs and documented atomic productions in c.bnf. Verified deterministic fuzz batches with SLATE_FUZZ_SEED=1,100,1000 and cargo fmt, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, cargo nextest r --release.

title: Expand atomic fixture coverage: explicit orderings, atomic_flag, non-int atomics
description:
Why: tests/fixtures/atomics.c only exercises seq_cst implicit-ordering int ops. The lowerer already maps mem_order/succ_order/fail_order attributes (rust_ordering/load_ordering/store_ordering in src/lower.rs) and has fallback paths for float/pointer atomics and an atomic_flag struct definition, but none of that surface is pinned by a fixture.

What to do: add C fixtures covering (a) atomic_*_explicit variants across relaxed/acquire/release/acq_rel orderings (respecting Rust's panics: no Release loads, no Acquire stores — load_ordering/store_ordering clamping should be exercised), (b) atomic_flag_test_and_set/clear, (c) the non-atomic RMW fallback for _Atomic float/pointer (single-threaded so behavior is well-defined), (d) atomic ops on unsigned/long/char widths mapping to AtomicU32/AtomicI64/AtomicI8 etc. Keep every fixture deterministic and single-threaded so differential output is stable. Fix whatever these fixtures flush out in baseline lowering.

Verify: each new fixture passes differential testing.
acceptance_criteria:
- New fixtures under tests/fixtures/ for explicit orderings, atomic_flag, float/pointer fallback, and multiple integer widths.
- All pass cargo nextest r --release.
- Any latent lowering bugs found get fixed in src/lower.rs (not fixups).
close_reason: Added atomic fixtures covering explicit orderings, atomic_flag operations, float/pointer fallback shapes, and multiple integer atomic widths, with output-shape assertions in tests/differential.rs. Verified with cargo fmt, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Prune unused stdatomic support items (memory_order, atomic_flag)
description:
Why: including <stdatomic.h> makes Slate emit the memory_order enum and atomic_flag struct as top-level items even when nothing in the generated program references them (both are dead in atomics.rs — orderings lower directly to std::sync::atomic::Ordering).

What to do: drop generated top-level items with no remaining references after all other fixups run — either a general unused-item pruning fixup (a top-level analog of dead_locals.rs) or by skipping known stdatomic header types at lowering when unreferenced. Prefer the general fixup: other header-borne types likely have the same problem. Must be reference-driven, not name-driven, so a program that genuinely uses memory_order as a value type keeps the enum.

Verify: atomics.rs no longer contains the enum/struct; fixtures that do reference header types still compile; full suite green.
acceptance_criteria:
- Unused memory_order/atomic_flag items disappear from atomics.rs.
- Items with any remaining reference are kept.
- cargo nextest r --release passes.
close_reason: Implemented a reference-driven unused top-level type item pruning pass for enums/records/structs, removing dead stdatomic memory_order and atomic_flag while keeping referenced types. Verified with cargo fmt, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: I2: Clean irreducible prologue/exit around residual loop{match}
description: With structuring running early, confirm goto_irreducible's reducible entry-branch and trailing done block collapse and redundant x=0; / _v3 temp are removed by existing passes now that they see ordinary code. If a redundancy survives, trace the responsible pass (likely inline_temps/zero_init ordering) rather than special-casing in rewrite::goto. Residual loop{match} over the 2-entry SCC stays.
acceptance_criteria: goto_irreducible: no redundant x=0; single let __blockN prologue; _v3 inlined; loop{match} retained; differential green.
close_reason: Redundant 'x = 0' now dropped: generalized zero_init to remove a constant store (value reads nothing) past any effectful statement that doesn't touch the binding, gated to the late pass (cross_effects) so it doesn't fuse __retval before return-slot lowering. Single 'let mut __block0' prologue and loop{match} retained; differential green with a new no-'x = 0' assertion. _v3 volatile-read temp intentionally kept — inline_temps never inlines VolatileRead (does_not_inline_impure_intrinsics); that boundary is correct.

title: I3: Reducible goto fixtures + document structuring boundary
description: Add reducible fixtures the suite lacks (nested if-with-goto, multi-exit loop, switch-with-goto forward jumps). Assert goto_if_scope/goto_return_value are branch-structured; keep computed_goto_ops and add a truly-irreducible case asserting the loop{match} fallback survives. Update slate-04q.40.6 doc: reducible => structured, irreducible/computed => dispatch.
acceptance_criteria: New fixtures pass differential; shape assertions cover structured + fallback; boundary documented.
close_reason: Added reducible goto fixtures for nested-if, multi-exit loop, and switch-forward jumps; extended goto structuring for switch transfers and multi-exit self-loops; asserted structured reducible output and computed/irreducible fallback boundaries. Docs intentionally skipped per user instruction. Verified with cargo fmt, cargo test generated_differential -- --nocapture, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Widen remaining cleanup fixups through match-arm bodies
description:
Why: zero_init, call_args, and nullable_pointer still have narrower bespoke traversal than the shared fixup walkers. Dispatch fallback match arms can hide cleanup opportunities from these passes.

What to do:
- Audit zero_init, call_args, and nullable_pointer traversal.
- Prefer shared nested-body walkers where path-sensitive facts require it.
- Add focused match-arm tests for each changed pass.
- Preserve existing semantic guardrails; this is traversal widening only.
acceptance_criteria:
- zero_init reaches eligible patterns inside match arms.
- call_args reaches eligible patterns inside match arms.
- nullable_pointer reaches eligible patterns inside match arms when its existing facts prove the rewrite.
- cargo fmt and cargo test pass.
close_reason: Widened zero_init, call_args, and nullable_pointer traversal through shared nested-body walkers so match-arm bodies are covered. Added focused match-arm tests for all three passes. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo test.

title: Expand goto fixture coverage for structured and fallback lowering
description:
Why: CFG structuring must stay conservative. We need fixtures that prove supported reducible cases improve while unsupported cases still fall back correctly.

What to do:
- Add or update fixtures for simple backward loop, forward goto, nested/scope-sensitive goto, and irreducible or multi-entry control flow if CIR can express it.
- Add output-shape assertions for structured versus fallback paths.
- Keep differential execution as the correctness backstop.
acceptance_criteria: - Tests assert goto_backward_loop.c uses structured loop lowering.\n- Tests assert at least one unsupported goto fixture still uses __state/__dispatch.\n- Differential tests pass for all added fixtures.
close_reason: Added goto_irreducible.c and expanded dispatch/structured output assertions for backward loop, forward goto, nested goto, and irreducible fallback. Verified with cargo fmt, focused differential tests, generated_differential, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Audit cleanup fixups for dispatch match-arm coverage
description:
Why: inline_temps is the obvious gap, but other cleanup passes with hand-written traversal may also skip Stmt::Match arms, leaving fallback dispatch code unnecessarily raw.

What to do:
- Review compound_assign, retval/final_return_temps, drop_call_results, printf_format, main_zero_exit-adjacent cleanup, remove_mut, and dead_locals for match-arm traversal gaps.
- Prefer shared fixup walkers where possible.
- Add focused tests for any changed pass.
acceptance_criteria: - Every applicable cleanup pass either traverses Stmt::Match arms or documents why match arms are intentionally out of scope.\n- Tests cover at least one dispatch-style match arm for changed passes.
close_reason: Audited dispatch match-arm cleanup. Retval main-exit collapse is now path-aware for match arms and removes dead pure __retval writes after nested collapse; added match-arm coverage for retval, drop_call_results, printf_format, and documented main_zero_exit nested-exit behavior. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo test.

title: Lower CIR intrinsic escape hatch, EH setjmp, and vector ops
description:
Why: the remaining broad extension surfaces are the LLVM intrinsic escape hatch, EH-adjacent setjmp, and vector-extension ops. They need source fixtures before lowering choices are defensible.

Ops: `cir.call_llvm_intrinsic`, `cir.eh.setjmp`, `cir.vec.*`.

What to do:
- Add C fixture(s) or focused CIR probes that emit representative ops from LLVM intrinsic builtins, setjmp/EH-adjacent lowering, and C vector extensions.
- Split further if one subgroup turns out to require substantial independent lowering.
- Implement conservative lowering or intentional diagnostics for the discovered op shapes.
- Update docs/cir-op-prioritization.md.
acceptance_criteria:
- At least one representative fixture/probe is added for each subgroup, or a follow-up bead is filed with the exact blocker.
- Supported op shapes have direct tests and do not generate unsupported `todo!` output.
- Large subgroup-specific work is split before implementation if needed.
close_reason: Implemented CIR vector extension lowering for !cir.vector, #cir.const_vector, vector cir.add, cir.vec.extract, cir.vec.insert with constant index, and cir.vec.shuffle; added vector_extension_ops differential fixture and direct lowerer tests. Added direct cir.eh.setjmp initial-return lowering and deliberate cir.call_llvm_intrinsic panic fallback coverage; documented that this Clang emits plain setjmp as a returns_twice _setjmp call rather than cir.eh.setjmp. Verified with cargo fmt --check, focused lowerer tests, cargo nextest r --release --test differential generated_differential --nocapture, cargo nextest r --release, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, and post-merge cargo fmt && cargo test.

title: Lower CIR target cache, prefetch, frame, and stack builtins
description:
Why: target/cache and frame/stack builtins remain listed as unsupported P3 CIR hooks. They need concrete fixtures and conservative Rust behavior.

Ops: `cir.clear_cache`, `cir.prefetch`, `cir.frame_address`, `cir.stacksave`, `cir.stackrestore`.

What to do:
- Add C fixture(s) that actually emit these CIR ops, likely from `__builtin___clear_cache`, `__builtin_prefetch`, `__builtin_frame_address`, and stack save/restore builtins if Clang CIR exposes them.
- Decide per op whether Slate should lower to a no-op, libc/core intrinsic, raw pointer value, or explicit unsupported diagnostic.
- Add synthetic lowerer coverage for direct op spellings when needed.
- Update docs/cir-op-prioritization.md.
acceptance_criteria:
- Fixtures or documented CIR probes establish the emitted op shape for each targeted builtin.
- Implemented ops do not leak unsupported temps into generated Rust.
- Behavior is covered by tests or documented as an intentional diagnostic path.
close_reason: Implemented cir.clear_cache, cir.prefetch, cir.frame_address, cir.stacksave, and cir.stackrestore lowering in src/lower.rs; added target_stack_builtin_ops fixture for frontend-emitted clear_cache/prefetch/frame_address; added direct CIR coverage for stacksave/stackrestore because this Clang does not recognize __builtin_stack_save/__builtin_stack_restore; updated docs/cir-op-prioritization.md. Verified with cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, cargo fmt, cargo run -- emit-fixtures, cargo nextest r --release, and post-merge cargo fmt && cargo test.

title: Lower CIR inline assembly and labels-as-values extensions
description:
Why: GNU-style extensions for inline assembly and computed goto remain unsupported and can appear in systems C.

Ops: `cir.asm`, `cir.block_address`.

What to do:
- Add C fixture(s) that emit these CIR ops, likely from inline `asm` and labels-as-values/computed-goto source.
- Implement the best available Rust lowering, feature-gated inline assembly, or precise diagnostics when semantics cannot be preserved.
- Add synthetic lowerer coverage for direct op spellings where source fixtures cannot run differentially.
- Update docs/cir-op-prioritization.md.
acceptance_criteria:
- Fixture/probe output shows `cir.asm` and/or `cir.block_address` shapes.
- Generated Rust is either valid for supported cases or fails through a deliberate diagnostic, not accidental `todo!` leakage.
- Docs reflect the supported/diagnostic status.
close_reason: Implemented cir.asm pass-through lowering for tied no-op inline asm, direct cir.block_address opaque pointer lowering, and computed-goto lowering for #cir.block_addr_info arrays plus cir.indirect_br dispatch. Added inline_asm_ops and computed_goto_ops differential fixtures, direct lowerer coverage, and docs update. Verified with cargo fmt --check, focused cargo test lowerer cases, cargo nextest r --release --test differential generated_differential --nocapture, cargo nextest r --release, and post-merge cargo fmt && cargo test.

title: Lower CIR control-flow prediction and unreachable builtins
description:
Why: branch prediction, assumptions, traps, and unreachable paths are remaining P3 CIR ops that Clang can emit from builtins and optimization hints.

Ops: `cir.assume`, `cir.expect`, `cir.trap`, `cir.unreachable`.

What to do:
- Add C fixture(s) that actually emit these CIR ops, likely from `__builtin_assume`, `__builtin_expect`, `__builtin_trap`, and `__builtin_unreachable`.
- Implement lowering or intentional diagnostics preserving observable behavior.
- Add synthetic lowerer coverage for direct op spellings when frontend fixtures fold or erase an op.
- Update docs/cir-op-prioritization.md.
acceptance_criteria:
- Fixture generation proves the targeted CIR ops appear, or the ticket documents the exact frontend spelling that supersedes them.
- Differential or focused tests cover supported behavior.
- No targeted op remains as an unsupported `todo!` in generated Rust for the fixture.
close_reason: Implemented cir.assume, cir.expect, cir.trap, and cir.unreachable lowering in src/lower.rs; added control_flow_builtin_ops differential fixture and direct lowerer coverage; updated docs/cir-op-prioritization.md. Verified with cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, cargo fmt, cargo run -- emit-fixtures, cargo nextest r --release, and post-merge cargo fmt && cargo test.

title: Elide redundant VaList clone for simple va_start locals
description:
Why: simple variadic functions currently emit a hidden variadic parameter plus a local VaList initialized with __slate_va_args.clone(), e.g. let mut ap: VaList; ap = __slate_va_args.clone();. For the common C shape va_list ap; va_start(ap, last); ... va_arg(ap, T); va_end(ap);, generated Rust can be closer to C by naming the Rust variadic parameter ap and using it directly.

What to do:
- Detect the simple case with one va_list local initialized by va_start and consumed by va_arg, with no competing va_start targets or ambiguous uses.
- Emit the C va_list name as the variadic parameter name and avoid the local VaList declaration/clone assignment.
- Keep existing clone-based lowering for complex or ambiguous cases.
- Add/adjust an output-shape assertion for tests/fixtures/varargs.c so the simple sum function has no __slate_va_args.clone() boilerplate.

Acceptance criteria: varargs fixture still passes differential testing; the simple sum generated Rust uses mut ap: ... directly and does not emit ap = __slate_va_args.clone().
notes: touches: src/fixups/facts/mod.rs, src/fixups/facts/va_list.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/va_list.rs, src/fixups/mod.rs, tests/differential.rs
close_reason: Implemented a facts/rewrite pass that elides simple variadic VaList clone aliases and keeps clone-based lowering for multiple cursors or reassignment. Verified on work/slate-d15 before merge with cargo fmt, cargo test va_list -- --nocapture, cargo nextest r --release --test differential counted_varargs_loop_uses_range_for --no-capture, cargo nextest r --release --test differential generated_differential --no-capture, and cargo nextest r --release; post-merge rerun skipped by user request.

title: Lift counted va_arg loops to Rust for ranges
description:
Why: user-defined variadic functions currently lower C counted loops over va_arg as C-shaped while/loop control. For a shape like for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += va_arg(ap, int), generated Rust remains a manual loop even though the trip count is explicit and the va_arg consumption is one side effect per iteration. This is correct but less idiomatic than for _ in 0..n { sum += unsafe { ap.next_arg::<i32>() }; }.

What to do:
- Extend the counted-loop/for-loop fixup path to accept loops whose body consumes a VaList via next_arg when the loop index is only used for trip counting.
- Preserve ordering and exactly one va_arg consumption per iteration; skip cases where the index is used semantically, the va_list is advanced conditionally, or the body has ambiguous control flow.
- Add an output-shape assertion for tests/fixtures/varargs.c showing the sum loop becomes a Rust for range while differential behavior stays unchanged.
- Keep baseline lowering unchanged; this is an optional AST-to-AST fixup.
acceptance_criteria: tests/fixtures/varargs.c generated Rust uses a for range for the counted va_arg sum loop. Cases with index-dependent body behavior or conditional va_arg consumption remain on the baseline loop path. cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release pass.
close_reason: Implemented a generalized CountedLoopFact and range_loop rewrite that lifts canonical counted loops to Rust 0..bound for loops, with the varargs fixture asserting the range form. Verified with cargo fmt, cargo test range_loop -- --nocapture, cargo nextest r --release --test differential counted_varargs_loop_uses_range_for --no-capture, cargo nextest r --release --test differential generated_differential --no-capture, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Idiomize fgets on owned FILE handles
description: Build on FILE ownership facts to rewrite eligible fgets patterns from raw libc calls into std::io reading APIs. Handle common line-buffer use first, preserving C behavior around maximum byte count, trailing newline, NUL termination, and null return on EOF/error where the generated code observes it.
acceptance_criteria: Eligible fgets loops or single-line reads use BufRead/read_line or read_until-style Rust code. Fixtures cover line iteration, fixed-size buffers, EOF handling, and cases that must remain raw.
close_reason: Implemented fgets-loop idiomization: while(fgets(...)!=NULL){fputs(buf,stdout);} on owned FILE* now rewrites to a BufReader+Read::take-capped read_until loop. Fixed two latent bugs found via differential testing: fixup_body's sequential index-based plan application (broke with 2+ owners per function) and loop_mentions_any_handle missing loop-local alias growth (let unrecognized handle uses escape detection). Fixtures: stdio_gets_loop_{lines,truncation,eof,unsupported}.c. All 582 tests pass.

title: Idiomize fread and fwrite on owned FILE handles
description: Build on FILE ownership facts to rewrite eligible fread/fwrite calls into std::io::Read and Write operations. Preserve C item-count semantics, partial reads/writes, size/count multiplication, and observed return values.
acceptance_criteria: Eligible binary file read/write fixtures emit std::io::Read/Write code and remain differential. Tests cover size == 1 byte buffers, multi-byte element counts, short read behavior, fwrite return use, and rejected unsafe aliasing cases.

title: Preserve fclose lifetime boundaries for rewritten FILE owners
description: The first stdio rewrite removes fclose for eligible fopen/fputs owners and relies on RAII at the enclosing Rust scope. That is idiomatic only when the C close happens at the same effective scope end. Add a rewrite/fact path that turns fclose into an explicit drop or scopes the owned file so close timing is preserved before later opens, removes, renames, or control-flow boundaries.
acceptance_criteria: Rewritten FILE owners preserve the observable close point when later filesystem operations may depend on it. Fixtures cover write-close-reopen and close-before-remove/rename. The simple end-of-scope case still emits no redundant close call.
close_reason: Implemented: fclose is now elided only when it's the tail statement of the owning body; otherwise it's rewritten to an explicit drop(handle) to preserve C's observable close point. Covered by unit tests in stdio.rs and two differential fixtures (stdio_file_write.c for write-close-reopen, new stdio_file_close_before_remove.c for close-before-remove). 579/579 nextest tests pass, clippy clean.

title: Run late cleanup after slice-loop rewrites
description: After slice-loop recovery rewrites counted loops into iterator for-loops, rerun or schedule existing cleanup passes late enough to remove newly-dead loop artifacts. In particular, ptr_len_slice_item currently emits a stranded `let len: i32 = items.len() as i32;` after the index loop disappears, and the rewritten loop body keeps an unnecessary singleton scope around `total += *item;`. Reuse existing dead-temp/dead-local and unnecessary-braces/singleton-scope cleanup where possible rather than adding slice-loop-specific string cleanup. Add output-shape coverage for the materialized-item fixture.
close_reason: Implemented late loop cleanup after slice/range loop rewrites: reruns singleton-scope cleanup and removes newly-dead length-derived locals from slice loop recovery. Added unit coverage plus ptr_len_slice_item output-shape assertions. Verified with cargo test dead_locals -- --nocapture, cargo test singleton_scopes -- --nocapture, cargo test ptr_len_slice_loop_uses_materialized_item_name -- --nocapture, cargo nextest r --release --test differential generated_differential --nocapture, cargo nextest r --release, cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features, and post-merge cargo fmt && cargo test.

title: Support enumerate for slice loops with live index uses
description: Extend counted slice loop facts beyond SliceIndexOnly so loops that need both the element and the induction variable can rewrite to iter().enumerate()/iter_mut().enumerate(). Preserve the original index semantics where needed, including casts from usize back to the original index type, and keep non-canonical or side-effectful bounds raw.

title: Use materialized item names for lifted slice for-loops
description: Refine slice-loop recovery so iterator for-loop patterns are only introduced when the source/lowered Rust already materializes an element local from items[i]. Use that real local name as the for-loop pattern and remove the index-only temp chain. Do not invent names from slice-name stemming; no-temp loops stay in counted-loop form until a range/enumerate pass exists.
close_reason: Changed slice-loop rewrite to only use real materialized element locals, removed slice-name stemming, left no-temp synthetic cases as counted loops, and added ptr_len_slice_item differential coverage. Verified with cargo nextest r --release and cargo fmt && cargo test.

title: Strengthen read-only lifted slice params from &mut [T] to &[T]
description: After ptr_len and slice-index/loop recovery, functions translated from C `T *items, int len` may still have `items: &mut [T]` and callsites may pass `values.as_mut_slice()` even when the function only reads the slice. Add facts/rewrite support to prove the lifted slice param is read-only and strengthen the signature/calls to `&[T]`/`as_slice()`. For the ptr_len_slice `sum` case, the end state should use an immutable slice parameter; mutating cases such as `bump` must remain `&mut [T]`.
acceptance_criteria:
Read-only lifted slice parameters become `&[T]`.
Callsites for strengthened params pass `as_slice()` or an immutable slice borrow.
Any assignment, mutable borrow, raw mutable pointer derivation, or mutation through the slice keeps `&mut [T]`.
Tests cover ptr_len_slice sum strengthening while bump remains mutable.
notes: follow-up: late remove_mut needs borrow-alias read-only method facts for shared slice methods like len/iter
close_reason: Reworked remove_mut to use BorrowAliasFact as its source of truth, deleted BindingMutabilityFact and its collector, reran remove_mut after slice rewrites, and added read-only method/deref-assignment coverage. Verified with cargo test remove_mut -- --nocapture, cargo test ptr_len -- --nocapture, cargo test generated_differential -- --nocapture, and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Lift immutable char arrays to C string literals
description: Recover immutable NUL-terminated char arrays as borrowed C string literals when their use chain does not require indexing, mutation, writable storage, or stack-array identity. Add a string recovery candidate for C strings, prove char-array literals/assigned literals are terminated ASCII C strings with no interior NUL and no indexed/mutated uses, rewrite the binding to a c"..." value, and rewrite pointer views to .as_ptr() casts. Use mem_memchr.c as the first generated-output consumer so char word[] = "abc" no longer renders as [97, 98, 99, 0] when it is only used through C-string-compatible pointer/value observations.
notes: touches: src/fixups/facts/mod.rs, src/fixups/facts/strings.rs, src/fixups/rewrite/string_lift.rs, tests/differential.rs
close_reason: Implemented BorrowedCStr string facts and late C string literal lift for immutable NUL-terminated char arrays. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Refine nullable pointer results into Option values
description:
Add a generic fixup proof/rewrite for nullable pointer-returning operations that can be represented as Option<T> when downstream uses do not require pointer identity.

First producer: lifted memchr callsites, where the natural value is Option<usize> from .position() or Some(index) for proven NUL searches. Future producers include strchr/strrchr and other pointer-returning libc/builtin operations where the result has a known semantic value.

Acceptance criteria:
- Add facts/proof for pointer-result use chains that are safe to keep as Option<T>.
- The rewrite is generic over the producer expression and Option payload, not memchr-specific.
- For null-only uses, rewrite null checks to .is_none()/.is_some() and eliminate intermediate c_void/raw pointer temporaries.
- Preserve pointer-producing map_or/null_mut when the result escapes, is dereferenced, is stored in an unknown pointer location, or otherwise needs pointer identity.
- Keep memchr as the first consumer and add/extend generated-output plus differential coverage for mem_memchr.c.
close_reason: Implemented a generic nullable pointer Option refinement pass with memchr coverage. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Add AST attributes to enum definitions
description:
Why: structs already carry Rust attributes in the AST via StructDef.attrs, but enum rendering still hardcodes #[repr(C)] and derives in codegen. That makes enums inconsistent with the structured AST model and makes future enum-specific attributes harder to add or preserve.

What to do:
- Add an attrs field to EnumDef matching the existing StructDef.attrs pattern.
- Populate enum attrs during lowering instead of hardcoding them in codegen.
- Update codegen to render EnumDef.attrs the same way it renders StructDef.attrs.
- Keep current generated enum output unchanged unless an intentional attribute-order convention already exists.
- Update tests that construct EnumDef directly and add focused coverage that enum attributes survive AST emission.

Acceptance criteria:
- EnumDef owns its Rust attributes rather than relying on enum-specific hardcoded codegen.
- Generated enums still emit #[repr(C)] and #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)] where they do today.
- Existing enum fixtures continue to compile and differential tests stay green.

acceptance_criteria:

Mutable counted loops over a lifted mutable slice render as `iter_mut()` or equivalent.
Loops that still need the index use `iter().enumerate()`/`iter_mut().enumerate()` only when the index has a real non-indexing use.
Non-canonical bounds, escaping index uses, multiple arrays, byte-count mem* lengths, and side-effectful bounds stay raw.
Differential/output-shape tests extend ptr_len_slice coverage for sum-like reads and in-place mutation.

title: Improve preprocessor cfg parsing and predicate coverage
description:
Why: the slate-lq0 epic established multi-config translation but maps only 7 predefined target/debug macros; everything else is reported as unmapped-macro or opaque-predicate and refused. This epic widens the recoverable predicate surface where a faithful, non-guessing Rust mapping exists — mechanical target-macro table growth and syntactic feature-flag transliteration of custom flags — without reopening the scoped-out combinatorial/value-macro cases.

Scope:
- Extend known_cfg with unambiguous OS/arch/width target macros.
- Transliterate single custom-macro #if chains to cfg(feature = ...), recovering both branches via the existing matrix.

Out of scope (unchanged from slate-lq0): value-carrying predicates (#if V > 3), compiler-identity macros, interacting/nested chains (2^N explosion), and macros that reshape types rather than gate whole items.
design: Successor to the closed slate-lq0 epic. Reuses plan_configs/pin_args/merge_variants and the known_cfg table; no new pass machinery.
acceptance_criteria: Children extend recoverable predicates only where the Rust mapping is unambiguous or a faithful syntactic transliteration; refusals and diagnostics remain for genuinely unrecoverable cases; docs table stays the source of truth.

title: Lower custom-macro #if chains to cfg(feature = ...), with bounded nesting
description:
Why: translate-cfg refuses any conditional region whose predicate is not in known_cfg, including project flags like #ifdef MY_FEATURE. The faithful transliteration keeps BOTH branches and gates them with a Cargo feature, mirroring the C — not pinning the macro in single-config mode (which drops the inactive branch). defined(FOO) -> cfg(feature = "foo") is a syntactic 1:1 mapping, not a semantic guess: a build passing -DMY_FEATURE now passes --features my_feature.

What to do:
- Map custom (unmapped) atoms to feature cfgs: defined(FOO) -> cfg(feature = "foo") (normalized/lowercased); #ifndef -> not(...); boolean combos within a predicate compose via all()/any()/not() (just pred_to_cfg recursing).
- Handle MULTIPLE independent top-level chains via per-region attribution: pin only that chain's atoms, leave others at their default active branch, and gate just the items in that chain's line range. Independent regions do not multiply.
- Handle SOME nesting, bounded so codegen stays fast: allow nested #if up to a cap on generated configurations (e.g. a max nesting depth / max total variant count). Beyond the cap, refuse with a clear diagnostic pointing at the region rather than exploding into a 2^N matrix.
- Keep refusing value-carrying predicates (#if FOO == 2) and macros that reshape types (e.g. _FILE_OFFSET_BITS) rather than gate whole items.
- Document the -D -> --features correspondence and the nesting/variant cap in docs/cfg-portability.md.

Out of scope: unbounded nested/interacting macro exploration; guessing which feature combinations are meaningful.
design: Successor work under slate-mt9. Boolean and/any/not within a predicate is free (pred_to_cfg recursion). Multiple/nested chains need per-region attribution instead of the current global merge_variants (which keys items globally and forces a product). The nesting cap bounds the variant count so generation time stays bounded; pick the cap by generated-config count, not just depth.
acceptance_criteria: Custom single-macro chains translate both branches behind #[cfg(feature = ...)] / not(...); multiple independent top-level chains each gate their own region without a cross product; nesting is supported up to a documented bound (depth/variant cap) and refused beyond it with a region-pointing diagnostic; generated Rust compiles under the relevant feature states; value-macro and type-reshaping cases still refuse.
close_reason: Implemented project macro cfg(feature) mapping, per-region translate-cfg planning for multiple and nested whole-item chains with a 16-variant cap, docs, and cfg fixtures. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Extend known_cfg with obvious OS/arch/width macros
description:
Why: translate-cfg/record-cfg only map 7 predefined macros to Rust cfgs (src/preprocess.rs known_cfg). Several common target macros have unambiguous Rust equivalents but are reported as unmapped-macro today, so portable code that gates on them is needlessly refused. These are mechanical additions, not semantic guesses.

What to do:
- Extend known_cfg with the obvious target mappings, e.g.:
  - _WIN64 -> windows (or target_pointer_width = "64" + windows as appropriate)
  - __FreeBSD__ -> target_os = "freebsd"; __ANDROID__ -> target_os = "android"; __unix__ / other unixes as sensible
  - __i386__ -> target_arch = "x86"; __riscv -> target_arch = "riscv64"; __powerpc__/__wasm__ etc.
  - endianness/pointer-width: __LP64__/_LP64 -> target_pointer_width = "64"; endian macros -> target_endian
- Add each mapping to the docs/cfg-portability.md table (source of truth is known_cfg).
- Add cfg fixtures / expected_cfgs.json entries covering the new predicates.

Out of scope: compiler-identity macros (__GNUC__, _MSC_VER), value comparisons, and libc feature-test macros. Only add mappings where the Rust cfg is unambiguous.
design: Follow-up from the slate-lq0 preprocessor-cfg epic (now closed). Pure table extension in known_cfg; no changes to the merge/refusal machinery.
acceptance_criteria: New target macros map to their Rust cfg in record-cfg and translate-cfg; docs table updated; fixtures assert the mappings; ambiguous macros still report unmapped-macro.
close_reason: Implemented target macro mappings in src/preprocess.rs; updated cfg portability docs and record-cfg/translate-cfg fixtures for OS, arch, pointer-width, unix, win64, and ARM endian predicates. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release.

title: Stress printf literal escaping around recovered conversions
description: Why: Rust format strings require escaping braces and have different literal rules, so recovered printf formats need coverage for percent runs, braces, quotes, and backslashes. What: add parser and differential fixture coverage for literal escaping around multiple supported conversions. Acceptance: generated Rust contains valid escaped format strings and output remains differential-test equivalent.

title: Support printf fixed-float width and flags
description: Why: %8.2f, %+8.2f, and %08.2f are common fixed-decimal forms and extend the existing %f / %.Nf support. What: map static width, sign, zero padding, and precision for %f where Rust formatting matches C behavior closely enough; keep unsupported or dynamic cases on libc fallback. Acceptance: focused tests cover width, sign, zero padding, precision, and rejected dynamic precision.

title: Support printf integer precision forms
description: Why: %.Nd and width-plus-precision integer forms are common in formatted output. What: evaluate safe mapping for static integer precision such as %.3d and %08.3d, including interactions with sign and width flags, and reject unsupported dynamic precision. Acceptance: parser tests and differential fixtures cover supported precision, width interactions, and rejected star precision.

title: Evaluate printf string width and precision recovery
description: Why: %s width and precision are common, but C precision is byte-based while Rust string precision is character-based. What: add only semantics-preserving cases, likely width for recovered string literals first and precision only for known ASCII constant strings or via a helper. Acceptance: tests demonstrate safe supported cases and explicit rejection of byte/Unicode-ambiguous cases.

title: Support printf alternate-form integer prefixes
description: Why: %#x, %#X, and %#o are common debug formats and have direct Rust formatting equivalents. What: accept the alternate form flag for hex and octal integer conversions, compose it with already-supported static width where valid, and reject ambiguous unsupported combinations. Acceptance: parser tests and fixtures cover lower/upper hex, octal, width interactions, and unsupported cases.
close_reason: Implemented exact printf alternate integer prefix recovery for %#x, %#X, and %#o in src/fixups/printf_format.rs, including zero-value handling and static width/zero/left alignment via single-evaluation format! block arguments. Added printf_alternate_integer fixture and differential output-shape assertions. Verified with cargo fmt and cargo nextest r --release on main (197 passed).

title: Support printf pointer display conversion
description: Why: %p is common in low-level debug output and can usually map to Rust pointer formatting. What: evaluate and implement conservative %p recovery for pointer-valued arguments, preserving libc fallback when argument shape is not safely representable. Acceptance: add supported and rejected fixtures plus output-shape assertions.

close_reason: Implemented conservative printf %p recovery in src/fixups/printf_format.rs with pointer-typed argument checks, supported/rejected fixtures, and output-shape assertions. Verified with cargo test --test differential -- --nocapture and cargo nextest r --release.

description: Why: fixtures.cfg/*.c currently have no rendered Rust counterpart, so there is no easy way to eyeball the C and generated multi-config Rust side by side. What: extend 'slate emit-fixtures' to run translate-cfg on each top-level tests/fixtures.cfg/*.c (skipping reject/) and write tests/fixtures.cfg.generated/*.rs; gitignore that directory like the other generated dirs.

title: Evaluate printf floating-point macro recovery
description:
Why: %f and precision formats appear in many fixtures, but libc printf and Rust formatting can differ in rounding, locale, special values, and long-double handling.

What to do:
